questions.prompt: What is return on invested capital, why do investors care about it more than growth, and what are its limitations?
questions.ideal_answer: Return on invested capital is net operating profit after tax divided by invested capital, where invested capital is the operating capital the business actually employs, typically total debt plus equity less excess cash, or equivalently net working capital plus net fixed assets plus operating intangibles. It measures how much operating profit the business generates per dollar of capital it uses, before financing decisions. Investors care because it determines whether growth creates or destroys value. When ROIC exceeds the weighted average cost of capital, every dollar reinvested creates value and growth compounds; when ROIC is below WACC, growth destroys value and the company would be better returning capital to shareholders. A high-growth business earning below its cost of capital is destroying value faster the faster it grows, which is why growth alone is a poor investment thesis. A persistently high ROIC is also evidence of a competitive moat, since capitalism should compete excess returns away, so a business sustaining twenty-five percent returns for a decade is telling you something structural about its position. The limitations are real. It uses book capital, which understates the true capital base for a company that has expensed rather than capitalised its most valuable investments in research, brand, or software, so asset-light businesses can show artificially high ROIC. Acquisitions inflate invested capital through goodwill, so a serial acquirer's ROIC understates operating performance while a company that wrote off goodwill shows a flattered figure. It is a single-period measure so it says nothing about the returns on capital being invested today, which is what actually matters going forward, and incremental ROIC is often the more useful number. It is distorted by the age of the asset base, since depreciated assets shrink the denominator. And it is not meaningful for financial institutions.

expected_concepts.label: NOPAT over invested capital
Growth creates value only when ROIC exceeds WACC
Persistently high ROIC is evidence of a competitive moat
Book capital understates expensed intangible investment
Acquisition goodwill distorts comparability
Incremental ROIC matters more than the historical average
The age of the asset base distorts the denominator

common_mistakes.label: Confusing ROIC with return on equity, which is post-leverage
Not comparing ROIC against the cost of capital
Treating the reported figure as directly comparable across companies

rubric.scoring_notes: Three-part question. The ROIC-versus-WACC point is essential; at least two credible limitations are needed for Strong.

questions.prompt: What red flags would make you doubt a company's reported numbers?
questions.ideal_answer: I would group them. On the reconciliation between earnings and cash: net income persistently exceeding cash flow from operations, rising days sales outstanding, inventory growing faster than revenue, and a widening gap between reported and adjusted figures where the add-backs are recurring rather than genuinely one-off. On revenue recognition: unusual or lengthening payment terms, revenue recognised well ahead of delivery, growing unbilled or contract-asset balances, large fourth-quarter concentration, and related-party revenue. On the balance sheet: goodwill and intangibles that dominate assets with no impairment despite a falling share price, capitalisation of costs that peers expense, frequent restructuring charges that never end, and reserve or allowance balances that move conveniently against earnings pressure. On disclosure and governance: frequent changes of auditor or chief financial officer, late filings, material weaknesses in internal control, restatements, an auditor whose size is disproportionate to the company, complex structures in low-transparency jurisdictions, aggressive management compensation tied to short-term earnings, and heavy insider selling. On the narrative: reported results that never miss guidance, unusually smooth earnings in a volatile industry, and an accounting profile that diverges from close competitors with no operational reason. None of these is proof on its own, and each has innocent explanations. What matters is the cluster and the trend, and specifically whether a plausible business explanation exists and holds up. My method would be to compare against the closest peers first, since accounting choices that differ from an entire industry are the highest-signal observation available, then read the footnotes and critical audit matters in full, then work the earnings-to-cash reconciliation for the last several years, and finally see whether management's explanations for each anomaly are consistent with each other over time.

expected_concepts.label: Persistent gap between net income and operating cash flow
Receivables or inventory growing faster than revenue
Add-backs and restructuring charges that recur every year
Capitalising costs that peers expense
Auditor or CFO turnover, restatements, control weaknesses
Earnings that are implausibly smooth or always meet guidance
Comparing accounting choices against close peers as the primary method
No single flag is proof; the cluster and trend matter

common_mistakes.label: Listing flags with no method for weighing them
Treating any single flag as proof of manipulation
Covering only financial ratios and ignoring governance signals

rubric.scoring_notes: Breadth across categories plus a method. The peer-comparison instinct and the refusal to treat one flag as proof are what mark a Strong answer.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a recent deal you have followed. Why did it happen, and do you think it was a good deal for the acquirer?
questions.ideal_answer: A strong answer names a specific, recent, real transaction and gives the essential facts accurately: the parties, roughly the size, the consideration structure, and roughly when it was announced. It then explains the strategic rationale from the acquirer's point of view in concrete terms, whether that is buying capability the acquirer could not build fast enough, consolidating a fragmented market for cost synergies, acquiring distribution or a customer base, defending against a competitive threat, or deploying capital where the seller was a forced or motivated seller. It should say something about the valuation, at least directionally, comparing the multiple paid or the premium to where the sector trades and to precedent deals, and say whether it looks full. Then it takes a clear position on whether the deal was good for the acquirer and defends it with specific reasoning, ideally naming what would have to be true for the deal to work, such as achieving a stated synergy number, and what the main risk is, whether that is integration, regulatory approval, financing conditions, or paying at the top of a cycle. It should acknowledge the strongest argument against its own view. What distinguishes a strong answer is not which deal is chosen but the presence of an actual opinion supported by specifics, and the ability to say what would change that opinion.

expected_concepts.label: Names a specific, real, recent transaction with accurate facts
Explains why the acquirer did it, in concrete terms
Says something about the price paid relative to comparables or precedents
Takes a clear position rather than hedging
Identifies the main risk to the thesis
Acknowledges the strongest argument against their view

common_mistakes.label: Describing a deal without taking a position
Vague or inaccurate deal facts
Generic rationale such as 'synergies' with nothing specific

rubric.scoring_notes: Grade the reasoning, not the deal choice, and do not penalise a candidate for picking a deal outside the grader's knowledge. Reward a clear defended position and the acknowledgement of a counterargument. Penalise the absence of any opinion.

questions.prompt: Interest rates rise 200 basis points. Walk me through the effect on M&A and LBO activity.
questions.ideal_answer: The mechanical effects run through valuation and financing. Higher risk-free rates raise the discount rate in every DCF, which lowers present values, and they lower the multiple the market will pay, particularly for long-duration assets where more of the value sits far in the future. Higher borrowing costs directly reduce what a leveraged buyer can pay: debt is more expensive to service, so lenders will advance fewer turns of EBITDA at a given coverage ratio, the sponsor's equity cheque has to grow for the same purchase price, and IRRs fall for any given entry multiple. Sponsors respond by bidding less, so LBO activity typically falls faster and further than strategic M&A. Strategic buyers are less affected because they often have cash and lower financing needs, and their relative advantage over sponsors grows, so the mix shifts toward strategics. Then the second-order effects. A bid-ask spread opens up, because sellers anchor on the valuations of the previous regime while buyers price the new cost of capital, and deal volume falls until sellers capitulate or are forced to transact. Existing portfolio companies with floating-rate debt see coverage deteriorate, which pushes some toward restructuring and creates distressed opportunities. Holding periods extend as sponsors wait for a better exit environment, which slows distributions to limited partners and eventually slows fundraising. Structures adapt, with more seller notes, earn-outs, preferred equity, and private credit filling the gap left by syndicated markets. The direction of causation matters too: rates usually rise because of inflation or growth, so the effect on any given company's earnings depends on whether it has pricing power, and a business that can pass through cost may be relatively more valuable in that environment even as its multiple compresses.

expected_concepts.label: Higher discount rates compress valuations
Lenders advance fewer turns; equity cheques rise
Sponsor returns fall at any given entry multiple
Strategic buyers gain relative advantage over sponsors
A bid-ask spread opens and volume falls until sellers adjust
Floating-rate portfolio companies come under pressure
Structures adapt with seller notes, earn-outs, and private credit
The reason rates rose affects earnings, not just multiples

common_mistakes.label: Covering valuation but not financing capacity
Missing the second-order effects on holding periods and fundraising
Treating the rate move as isolated from what caused it

rubric.scoring_notes: The chain from rates to debt capacity to equity cheque to IRR is the technical core. Second-order effects distinguish a Strong answer.

questions.prompt: A founder owns 100% of a $200m revenue business and asks whether to sell to a strategic buyer, sell to a private equity firm, or IPO. How would you advise them?
questions.ideal_answer: The right answer depends on what the founder actually wants, so I would start there rather than with the options. Do they want full liquidity now or to keep participating in the upside? Do they want to keep running the business, and for how long? How much do they care about the company's independence, the brand, and the employees? What is their view on the business's next phase and whether they are the right person to lead it? Then map the options. A strategic sale usually delivers the highest headline price because a strategic can pay for synergies, gives full liquidity immediately, and is the cleanest exit, but the founder typically loses control, the business is often absorbed and the brand may disappear, employees face redundancy where roles overlap, and any earn-out is at the mercy of an acquirer they no longer control. A private equity sale usually prices below a strategic but allows a partial exit with meaningful rollover equity, so the founder takes real money off the table while retaining a second bite that can be worth more than the first, keeps an operating role, and gains a partner with capital and a playbook for the next phase; the costs are leverage, loss of full control, a board, and a mandated exit in roughly five years on the sponsor's timetable. An IPO offers the highest theoretical valuation for a genuinely high-growth business, keeps independence and gives the founder continued control if the structure allows, but delivers limited immediate liquidity because of lock-ups and the poor optics of a founder selling down, imposes substantial public company cost and disclosure, exposes the business to quarterly scrutiny, and at $200m of revenue may not clear the scale and predictability bar for a good listing at all. I would also stress that the process choice is not binary: running a dual-track process preserves optionality and creates competitive tension, and the market environment at the moment of decision may matter more than the theoretical ranking. My advice would be conditional on the founder's answers, and I would say so explicitly rather than picking one.

expected_concepts.label: Starts with what the founder wants, not with the options
Strategic: highest price, full liquidity, loss of control and identity
PE: partial exit, rollover second bite, leverage and a five-year clock
IPO: independence but limited liquidity, cost, scrutiny, and a scale bar
Notes that $200m revenue may be small for a good IPO
A dual-track process preserves optionality and creates tension
Gives conditional advice rather than a single answer

common_mistakes.label: Choosing an option without establishing the founder's objectives
Comparing the options on price alone
Treating an IPO as freely available at this scale

rubric.scoring_notes: Tests client judgement. Starting with the founder's objectives is the single most important element; an answer that ranks the options on price alone is Needs Work regardless of technical accuracy.

questions.prompt: Why investment banking, and why now?
questions.ideal_answer: A strong answer is specific, honest, and evidenced by what the candidate has actually done. It gives concrete reasons rooted in the work itself rather than generic claims: exposure to how companies are valued and financed at a formative moment, the analytical rigour of the work, the pace and breadth of learning across industries and transaction types, and the responsibility given early. It connects those reasons to specific evidence from the candidate's own experience, whether a valuation project, an internship, a student investment fund, a case competition, or independent work on a company they have researched, and shows what they learned from it rather than just naming it. It demonstrates a realistic understanding of what the job actually involves day to day, including the hours, the volume of process work, and the fact that a junior spends far more time on execution and materials than on strategic advice, and it explains why the candidate wants it anyway. The 'why now' half should be answered directly, tying to where they are in their studies, what they have already tested about their fit, and what specifically they want to be doing in the next two to three years. Weak answers rely on prestige, compensation, or generic phrases such as wanting to work with smart people or being passionate about finance, without any evidence. The bar is not eloquence; it is whether the reasons are specific enough that they could not be given by any other candidate.

expected_concepts.label: Specific reasons rooted in the nature of the work
Backed by concrete personal experience with what was learned
Realistic view of the day-to-day job including its downsides
Directly answers the timing half of the question
Says what they want to be doing in the next few years

common_mistakes.label: Generic answer that any candidate could give
Leading with prestige or compensation
Describing the junior role as primarily strategic advisory
Not answering the timing half at all

rubric.scoring_notes: Grade specificity and evidence, not polish or enthusiasm. Do not reward confident delivery of generic content. The test is whether the reasons could only have been given by this candidate.

questions.prompt: Pitch me a company you would buy today. What is the market missing, and what would prove you wrong?
questions.ideal_answer: A strong pitch has a clear structure. It names the company and states the recommendation and rough time horizon up front, then gives a short business description covering how the company actually makes money, its main segments, and its competitive position, so the listener has the context to judge what follows. It then states the variant perception explicitly: what the market believes, what the candidate believes instead, and why the market is wrong, which might be a misunderstood segment, a mispriced cyclical trough, an underappreciated structural change, an accounting artefact obscuring the true earnings power, or a temporary dislocation from a forced seller or index event. A thesis with no variant perception is not a thesis; it is a description of a good company, and good companies are usually priced as such. It supports the view with specific evidence and at least a rough valuation, whether a multiple against peers and history, an implied return, or a reverse DCF showing what the current price assumes and why that is too pessimistic. It names the catalyst or the mechanism by which the market comes to agree, and it is honest if there is no catalyst beyond time. Then the risks: the two or three specific things that would break the thesis, sized and stated as falsifiable conditions rather than a token disclaimer, and crucially what evidence would make the candidate change their mind. That last element is the strongest signal in the whole answer, because it separates someone holding a view from someone who has genuinely tested it. The quality of the pitch does not depend on the company chosen or on whether the grader agrees with the conclusion.

expected_concepts.label: States the company, the recommendation, and a horizon up front
Demonstrates real understanding of how the business makes money
Articulates what the market believes and why it is wrong
Supports the view with a valuation or implied return
Names a catalyst or is honest that there is none
Names specific, falsifiable risks rather than token caveats
States what evidence would change their mind

common_mistakes.label: Describing a good company without saying what the market is missing
Listing generic risks such as 'competition' or 'recession'
Making the case with no valuation anchor
A thesis with no condition that would disprove it

rubric.scoring_notes: Grade the structure and rigour, not the stock, and never penalise disagreement with the conclusion. The variant perception and the disconfirming-evidence element carry the most weight; a well-presented description of a quality company with neither is Developing at best.
